{"filepath":"research_findings.md","content":"Research findings — "Make it better" (preliminary)

Note: I did this initial market & web research using the provided clarifying_questions.md but no answers from the product owner were available. The findings below are therefore generic, prioritized opportunities for most digital product improvement projects (web / e‑commerce / SaaS). I’ll refine recommendations and estimates as soon as you provide the clarifying_questions.md answers or access to analytics/repo.

Executive summary
- Benchmarks: Core Web Vitals targets (LCP < 2.5s, FID/INP thresholds), industry cart abandonment ~70% (Baymard), usability ROI historically 83–135% (NN/g), accessibility baseline WCAG 2.1 AA.
- Quick wins (low effort, high impact): reduce largest contentful paint (LCP) by optimizing images & critical CSS; remove or defer 3rd‑party scripts; implement caching + CDN. Typical impact: measurable conversion lift (see studies below); estimated effort: hours–a few days.
- Bigger wins (medium effort): checkout flow simplification, server-side rendering/edge rendering, consolidate analytics/marketing tags. Typical impact: reduce cart abandonment, increase conversion and revenue; effort: 1–4 sprints.
- Strategic investments (higher effort): full frontend performance rewrite or progressive migration (component streaming, code splitting), full accessibility remediation, UX research + design sprints. Impact: sustained traffic and conversion improvements; effort: multiple sprints / months.

Benchmarks & evidence (selected sources)
- Core Web Vitals (targets & guidance): web.dev articles and Google Search docs. Key metrics: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP)/First Input Delay (FID legacy), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). (See: https://web.dev/articles/vitals, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals)
- Cart abandonment benchmark: Baymard Institute global average ~70.19% (2024 study and cart & checkout usability research). (See: https://baymard.com/research/checkout-usability and https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate)
- Usability ROI: Nielsen Norman Group — measured usability improvements averaged ~83% in a recent survey (previously 135%). Recommendation: invest ~10% of project budget in UX activities. (See: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/return-on-investment-for-usability and https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-roi-declining-but-still-strong)
- Page speed -> conversion: multiple case studies show substantial impact. Examples cited across studies: Amazon (1% sales per 100ms latency), Akamai (100ms → 7% conversion impact in some contexts), Google/Deloitte studies (milliseconds matter). Aggregate evidence: even small improvements (0.1s) can yield single-digit % conversion lifts depending on vertical. (See aggregator and examples: https://www.conductor.com/academy/page-speed-resources, https://www.portent.com/blog/analytics/research-site-speed-hurting-everyones-revenue.htm)
- Accessibility standard reference: WCAG 2.1 / 2.2 quick reference and techniques (W3C). Aim for at least AA for legal/commercial risk reduction and broader audience reach. (See: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21 and https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref)

Competitor / case study examples (representative)
- Vodafone: optimized Core Web Vitals and saw +8% sales (cited in speed case studies list).
- Yelp: improvements to FCP increased conversions by ~15% (case study lists).
- Amazon: internal tests found ~1% sales impact per 100ms of latency.
- Akamai / Ebay / Portent: multiple industry examples show meaningful revenue/engagement gains from performance tuning.
(Sources: Conductor’s page‑speed resources and aggregated case studies page: https://www.conductor.com/academy/page-speed-resources)

Common pain points observed across similar projects
- Slow LCP and long TTFB due to heavy images, render‑blocking CSS/JS, no CDN, or slow backend.
- High cart/checkout abandonment due to friction (too many steps, surprise costs, forced account creation, poor mobile UX).
- Excessive third‑party scripts (analytics, tag managers, A/B tests) causing latency and unpredictability.
- Poor accessibility (low color contrast, missing labels, keyboard issues) causing lost users and legal risk.
- Lack of instrumentation: insufficient real‑user monitoring (RUM), synthetic checks, and A/B measurement to quantify impact.

Prioritized opportunities (ranked by expected ROI vs effort)
1) Optimize LCP (images, critical CSS, server response)
   - Why: LCP is a Core Web Vital and strongly correlated with conversions.
   - Typical impact: improve conversions by single‑digit to low‑double‑digit % (studies show 8%+ per 0.1s in verticals; Amazon-style 1% per 100ms for commerce is a reasonable planning figure). Confidence: medium.
   - Effort: low–medium. Quick wins (image compression, format switching to WebP/AVIF, responsive images, set width/height to avoid layout shifts) — 1–5 developer days. Larger changes (SSR/edge rendering or backend tuning) — 1–4 sprints.
   - Dependencies: access to CMS/build pipeline, image library, devs with frontend/perf skills.

2) Audit and remove/defer third‑party scripts
   - Why: Many sites incur 20–40% of interaction latency from tags. Reducing tags improves INP/FID and LCP.
   - Typical impact: measurable speed + stability improvements; conversion uplift often 3–8%. Confidence: medium.
   - Effort: low. Audit + remove unused tags (1–3 days); implement Tag Manager sampling/defer + wrapper (1–2 sprints for robust solution).
   - Risks: possible loss of tracking data; mitigations include server‑side tag forwarding.

3) Simplify checkout flow / reduce friction
   - Why: Checkout usability is the highest ROI area for e‑commerce (Baymard research). Small UX fixes often produce outsized improvements in completed purchases.
   - Typical impact: reduce abandonment by multiple percent points; conversion improvement varies by baseline — could be 5–20% on checkout conversions. Confidence: medium‑high.
   - Effort: medium. Usability review + 1–2 experiments (A/B tests) — 2–6 weeks. Implementation of changes — 1–3 sprints.
   - Quick fixes: allow guest checkout, reduce form fields, show totals earlier, clear shipping/costs, add progress indicator.

4) Implement RUM + synthetic monitoring and set performance budgets
   - Why: Measurement is required to prioritize and prove impact; performance budgets prevent regressions.
   - Typical impact: enables ongoing improvements; helps quantify ROI. Confidence: high.
   - Effort: low–medium. Set up tools (Lighthouse CI, web-vitals library, New Relic/Sentry/Datadog Browser, or Google Analytics RUM) — 2–7 days. Integrate into CI/CD — 1–2 sprints.

5) Accessibility remediation to WCAG AA
   - Why: Broadens audience, reduces legal risk, improves UX; often uncovered issues are low effort to fix.
   - Typical impact: increased usable customer base, reduction in help tickets; qualitative improvements to conversions. Confidence: medium.
   - Effort: low–high depending on current state. Small fixes (labels, contrasts) — days to weeks. Large ARIA/interaction fixes or redesigns — months.

6) Consolidate & optimize frontend build (code splitting, tree shaking, lazy loading)
   - Why: Reduces JS payload, improves TTFB/LCP/INP.
   - Typical impact: material improvements to interactivity and loading; conversions improve proportionally. Confidence: medium.
   - Effort: medium–high (1–3 sprints) depending on tech stack.

Suggested quick wins (1–7 days each)
- Compress/serve images in modern formats (WebP/AVIF) and add responsive srcset. Effort: 1–3 days. Impact: large LCP improvement.
- Defer non‑essential JS and remove unused polyfills. Effort: 1–3 days. Impact: better INP/LCP.
- Implement server/edge CDN caching for static assets. Effort: 1–2 days if using managed CDN. Impact: lower TTFB and more predictable performance.
- Guest checkout + reduce form fields (UX change). Effort: 2–5 days (depends on backend). Impact: immediate drop in abandonment.

Measurement & success metrics (examples)
- Performance: LCP (target <2.5s), INP (target <200ms ideally), CLS (<0.1). Measure via RUM (Chrome UX Report, web-vitals) and Lighthouse.
- Business: conversion rate (overall and checkout funnel), cart abandonment rate (target reduce by X% — baseline needed), revenue per visitor, bounce rate, support tickets for checkout issues.
- Accessibility: % of pages passing WCAG 2.1 AA automated checks; number of outstanding manual WCAG issues.

Estimated timeline & sample plan (3–5 day discovery + prioritization)
Day 0–3: Discovery & instrumentation
- Collect analytics, RUM data, Lighthouse labs, checkout funnel metrics, list of third‑party tags, accessibility scan.
- Deliver: prioritized quick wins and backlog with estimated effort.

Sprint 1 (2 weeks): Execute 2–3 quick wins
- Image optimization, defer scripts, enable CDN, deploy RUM, implement guest checkout experiment.
- Measure RUM before/after and run A/B tests on checkout changes.

Sprint 2 (2 weeks): Medium efforts
- Implement critical CSS, lazy load below‑the‑fold components, reduce JS bundle size; apply WCAG fixes.

Ongoing: monitoring, incremental UX research, A/B testing high‑impact checkout changes.

Costs & resourcing (back‑of‑envelope)
- Quick wins: 8–40 developer hours each (~1–5 days). Product/Design/QA add similar time. Cost varies by internal rates.
- Medium changes: 1–2 developer sprints (2–4 weeks) per area (SSR, major checkout changes).
- Strategic rewrite/accessibility program: multiple sprints; estimate 2–6 months depending on scope.

Assumptions & next steps required from you (information I need to refine estimates)
1) Answer clarifying_questions.md (attach completed file) or at minimum tell me:
   - What exactly are we improving (site name, product, or flow)?
   - Primary KPIs/targets (conversion, revenue, Core Web Vitals, accessibility level).
   - Access: analytics, repo, staging site credentials.
   - Any hard deadlines or compliance requirements.
2) Provide current metrics: Lighthouse scores, Core Web Vitals RUM, checkout funnel conversion and abandonment rates, top entry pages.
3) If available, provide competitor URLs or existing UX research and backlog items.

Selected references and links
- Core Web Vitals / web.dev: https://web.dev/articles/vitals
- Google Search docs (Core Web Vitals): https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals
- Baymard Institute — checkout usability & cart abandonment: https://baymard.com/research/checkout-usability and https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate
- Nielsen Norman Group — ROI for usability: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/return-on-investment-for-usability and https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-roi-declining-but-still-strong
- WCAG quick reference / techniques: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21 and https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref
- Page speed case studies and resources (aggregator): https://www.conductor.com/academy/page-speed-resources
- Site speed research / Portent: https://www.portent.com/blog/analytics/research-site-speed-hurting-everyones-revenue.htm

Closing / ask
- If you want I can: (A) run a 3–5 day discovery with instrumentation and prioritized backlog; or (B) run an initial 1‑week sprint implementing the 2–3 quick wins listed above. Tell me which option and provide access to analytics/staging.

Prepared by: Research Specialist
Date: 06‑Sep‑2026

"}
